theme: The return decreed; the Temple foundation, joy and weeping
readingInstruction: Read Ezra 1:1-3:13. A pagan king releases the exiles, and a remnant returns to rebuild the temple. The chapter ends with a sound that is half laughter and half weeping. Read the last verses slowly.
settingTheScene: This is the final unit of the Old Testament. It covers about 150 years, from the decree of Cyrus in 538 BC to the close of the prophets around 400 BC. The exile ended just as Jeremiah said, after seventy years. Ezra and Nehemiah tell what happened next. Chronicles retells the whole story for the returned community. The theme of the unit is a partial return: God keeps his promises, but the full restoration is still to come.
observation: “In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus” (1:1).
“Whoever is among you of all his people, may his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem” (1:3).
Cyrus returned the temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken (1:7-11).
About 42,360 people returned, along with servants and singers (2:64-65).
“Then Jeshua… and his kinsmen… arose and built the altar of the God of Israel” (3:2).
“They set up the altar on its foundation, for fear was on them because of the peoples of the lands” (3:3).
“And they sang responsively, praising and giving thanks to the LORD, For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel” (3:11).
“Many of the priests and Levites and heads of fathers” houses, old men who had seen the first house, wept with a loud voice when they saw the foundation of this house’ (3:12).
interpretation:
Ezra begins by repeating the last verses of 2 Chronicles. God “stirred up the spirit of Cyrus,” the same Cyrus Isaiah had named by name 150 years earlier. The mightiest king in the world was moved by the LORD to send his people home. God works through pagan kings as easily as through prophets.

Only a remnant goes. Of the hundreds of thousands in exile, about 42,000 make the journey. Most stayed in Babylon, comfortable and settled. The ones who go are those whose spirits God stirred. Return costs something. The list in chapter 2 is full of names, as if to say that God knows each family who made that trip.

Their first act is not building a house for themselves. They build the altar. “For fear was on them because of the peoples of the lands,” yet they begin with worship. Then, in the second year, they lay the temple foundation. The priests blow trumpets, the Levites clash cymbals, and the people sing the refrain you met in Psalm 136: “He is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel.”

Then comes the strange mixture. Many shout for joy. But the old men who remembered Solomon’s temple weep aloud, because this foundation is so small by comparison. “The sound was heard far away.” No one could tell the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping. That is the mark of the whole unit. The return is real, and it is smaller than the promise. The people have come home, but they are still under Persia, and the glory has not yet returned. Joy and sorrow sit side by side, and both are right.
connection: Haggai 2:3 asks, “Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory?” Jesus began with small things: a mustard seed (Matthew 13:31-32). Zechariah 4:10 says, “Who has despised the day of small things?” Romans 8:23 says that we groan inwardly as we wait for redemption, though we have the first fruits of the Spirit. Philippians 1:6 promises that God who began a good work will bring it to completion.
application:
Where has God given you a beginning that seems small compared to what you hoped? Thank him for it anyway.

Build your altar first: begin your day or your project with worship.

Be honest that joy and sorrow can coexist. You do not have to choose only one.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to stir your spirit to go where he calls.
Thank him for bringing a remnant home.
Tell him what you want to rebuild.
